narrative:
The model predicts a 40% chance that you will fail your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help strengthen your performance before it is too late.

The decision rests mainly on three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed two classes in the past. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, your history of repeated setbacks strongly signals to the model that you are at serious risk of failing again.

Two other factors also pushed the prediction toward failure, though less forcefully. First, you come from a smaller family of three or fewer members. Most students who passed actually came from larger families, so your family size worked against you in the model’s eyes. Second, you did not attend nursery school. The majority of successful students had gone to nursery, making your lack of early education another element that nudged the outcome toward failing.

To turn this around, focus first on breaking the pattern of failure. Speak with your teachers about targeted support in the subjects that have caused problems before. Build consistent daily study habits, reduce time going out with friends if it cuts into revision, and use the extra remedial classes to close any remaining gaps. Small, steady improvements now can still change your final result.
